name: Entamoeba histolytica complex

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Cyst: usually 10–20 µm, up to four nuclei, fine peripheral chromatin and a small karyosome; chromatoid bodies may have rounded ends.
Trophozoites commonly 15–20 µm but range more widely; ingested erythrocytes support invasive E. histolytica but are not an absolute species rule.

transmission.detail: Mature cysts are ingested; trophozoites colonize the large intestine. E. histolytica can invade tissue and spread to the liver.

life_cycle.detail: Mature cysts are ingested; trophozoites colonize the large intestine. E. histolytica can invade tissue and spread to the liver.
Cysts or trophozoites in stool; tissue or aspirate findings belong to a distinct specimen category.

hosts: Humans are the principal clinical host; no intermediate host.
distribution: Worldwide, especially settings with fecal contamination; relevant throughout Southeast Asia.
clinical_significance: E. histolytica causes amoebic colitis and liver abscess. An unresolved complex is not a diagnosis of invasive amebiasis; morphologically similar organisms require different interpretation.
specimen: Cysts or trophozoites in stool; tissue or aspirate findings belong to a distinct specimen category.
diagnostics: Permanent stained smears near 1000× show nuclear features; iodine aids cyst assessment.
Species-specific antigen or molecular tests are needed to resolve the complex.
differential_diagnosis: E. histolytica, E. dispar and E. moshkovskii cannot reliably be separated by routine microscopy.
Compare mature nuclear count with E. coli and use calibrated size for small amoebae.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
